brief.situation: You administer web02, a RHEL-family web server with SELinux enforcing at Fernhill Books (fictional). At 09:50 a developer moved the new documentation site from /home/deploy/site into /var/www/html/docs with mv. Since then https://fernhill.example/docs/ answers 403 Forbidden. At 10:45 the release email goes to 40,000 customers with links to the docs. Find out why the web server cannot read the files and fix it without weakening the server.
handover: httpd serves /var/www/html. The rest of the site still works.
The developer says 'the permissions are fine, I checked with ls -l'.
howItWorks: Run commands from the command line: type one, or pick it from the suggestions or the action list. Only this lab's commands run; there is no free shell, and each command's arguments come from its list.
Each command takes operator time: run it, then let it finish, which moves the clock by the minutes it takes. The outage keeps developing on the same clock.
The map shows each host, device or service and the links between them, with a status in words. Output appears in the terminal as it happens.
When you declare the service restored, you write the incident record and explain your reasoning.

writeup.question: For the incident record: why the site answered 403 when ls -l looked fine, how you proved it, and why your fix is the right one.

parts.label: Cause
parts.criteria: Names the SELinux type: mv kept user_home_t from the home directory, which httpd_t may not read; ordinary permissions were fine.
parts.modelAnswer: mv keeps a file's SELinux label, so the moved files stayed user_home_t. httpd runs as httpd_t, which policy does not let read home-directory content, so the kernel denied it although rw-r--r-- allowed reading.

parts.label: Evidence
parts.criteria: Uses the audit log (ausearch -m AVC) or ls -Z before changing anything; does not infer SELinux from the 403 alone.
parts.modelAnswer: ausearch showed an AVC denial for httpd_t on index.html with tcontext user_home_t, and ls -Z showed the moved files with that type.

parts.label: Fix
parts.criteria: Restores the default label with restorecon -R (the path's default is httpd_sys_content_t); keeps SELinux enforcing and the permissions as they were; explains why setenforce 0 or chmod 777 is not a fix.
parts.modelAnswer: restorecon -Rv set the files to the path's default type, httpd_sys_content_t, with SELinux still enforcing. Permissive mode would switch protection off for every service, and 777 would let anything on the box rewrite the site while still being denied.

expertPath.text: Confirm the 403 and read the error log: 'Permission denied' from the kernel.
ls -l is fine; ls -Z shows user_home_t; ausearch -m AVC shows httpd_t denied reading user_home_t.
restorecon -Rv /var/www/html/docs, then curl /docs/ for a 200, SELinux still enforcing.
Record mv keeping the home-directory label as the cause; suggest cp, or restorecon in the deploy script.

scoring.modelReasoning: A 403 right after an mv into the web root, with ordinary permissions that allow reading, points at SELinux labels: mv keeps user_home_t, which httpd_t may not read. Confirm with ausearch -m AVC (or ls -Z), run restorecon -Rv on the moved directory to restore the default httpd_sys_content_t, keep SELinux enforcing and the permissions unchanged, and verify with a request.
